subject: Acme integration: post-call recap + request/response schema questions

Subject: Acme integration — post-call recap + open questions

Hi Samir / Elena,

Thanks again for the time this morning — great conversation. Quick recap and a short list of follow-ups so our engineers can draft an integration plan:  

1) Integration scope: you want SDK-based server-side calls from our Dedicated environment to support: 1) chat-based conversational assistants for customer support, 2) embeddings for semantic search over product docs, and 3) a lightweight reranker to boost relevant results.
2) Auth & infra: Acme prefers short-lived credentials via your existing service account model (we discussed SAML SSO + service principal).
3) Schema & outputs: you asked about structured outputs (JSON/tool-calling) vs free-text completions, and concerns about tokenization / truncation behavior for long contexts.

Open questions: 
- Preferred approach for chat vs completions for your use cases? (we gave examples but wanted your priority)
- Any hard limits on response size or stop sequences we should enforce?
- Do you plan to stream responses to the browser client, or will server aggregate then send?
- Any constraints for embeddings (batch size, fields to hash, vector store choices)?

Next steps: Neha will provide a short technical note that covers SDK auth patterns, routing/fallback, structured output options, and token accounting. Marcus will share the integration guide and an example RSP schema. We’ll coordinate a follow-up tech call next week to go deeper.

Thanks — Marissa

--
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.ai | +1 415-555-0132

Hi Marissa / team,

Thanks for the recap — this looks right. To answer the open questions from our side: 

- Priority: Chat-based assistants are highest priority (support flow + triage). Embeddings for search are next. Reranker is optional but desirable for Q4.
- Response size: we need predictable max length for transcripts stored in our DB; target max tokenized output ~1500 tokens but we can start with 800 if that’s safer.
- Streaming: ideally we stream tokens to our web app for the live assistant UI. If not possible initially, server-side aggregation is acceptable.
- Embeddings: we plan to batch documents nightly (10k docs) and update vectors incrementally. We use Pinecone today but open to alternatives.

We’re comfortable with SAML + short-lived keys; our security team will want a short tech note for the procurement/security questionnaire.

Samir
Director of Platform, Acme Corp

Hi Samir / Elena — great notes. Below is a concise technical breakdown addressing the items you raised. Happy to expand on any section in the follow-up call.

1) SDK setup & auth
- SDK: our server-side SDK supports chat and completions endpoints. For node/python we provide helpers to stream deltas (server-sent events / websockets) or to return aggregated responses.
- Auth: we support API keys (long-lived) and short-lived tokens via our SSO/service-principal flow (recommended for Dedicated/Private deployments). We can exchange a SAML assertion for a short-lived bearer token scoped to the service principal; tokens are valid for configurable TTL (default 1h).
- KMS/HSM: customer-managed key support available for Private deployments; we list required roles/SCIM groups in the attachment.

2) Routing & fallback
- You can route by region/model/capacity tier. Example policy: prefer low-latency model in us-west, fallback to a compatible quantized variant if Dedicated capacity is temporarily constrained.
- For embeddings batch jobs, we recommend routing to a high-throughput embedding-optimized node pool and using our batch API (multipart) to avoid excessive per-request overhead.

3) Structured output / tool calling
- Tool calling: our chat endpoint supports function/tool calls. You define a JSON schema for each tool’s args; the model returns a function call with name + args or regular assistant content. The SDK will either execute the tool (if you wire it) or return the call for your code to handle.
- JSON enforcement: we provide a response_format option (schema + strict flag). In strict mode we will keep prompting and retrying until the output parses as valid JSON or hit a retry budget. This is useful for deterministic downstream parsing.

4) Chat vs completions (key differences relevant to you)
- Chat: message-based input (system/user/assistant role tokens are counted). Better for multi-turn state, tool calling, and structured responses. Chat streaming returns deltas (role + content) that map cleanly to incremental UI updates.
- Completions: single prompt string, simpler for legacy integrations; may be marginally cheaper for single-turn generation but lacks structured tool-calling primitives.
- Tokenization accounting: tokens include prompt + response + special tokens (system/etc.). For chat we count all messages in the context window. Use our tokenizer utility in the SDK to estimate before sending long contexts.

5) Token limits, max_tokens, and stop semantics
- max_tokens: controls the max tokens for the model output (not counting prompt). If you set 800, the model won’t exceed that for the completion, but truncation can happen if total tokens exceed the model’s context window.
- Stop sequences: supported on both endpoints. For chat, stop sequences are applied to the assistant's reply; you can pass multiple sequences. If streaming, we still stream tokens until we detect a stop sequence and then send a final event marking completion.
- Truncation: our SDK truncates earliest user/system messages by default (LRU-like) and provides heuristics to keep system instructions. You can override with explicit context selection.

6) Streaming semantics and client UX
- Two modes: server-stream (SDK streams to your server then you relay to client) or direct-stream (your client holds a short-lived token and streams directly to Redwood). Direct-stream reduces server cost and latency but requires secure short-lived tokens.
- Streaming guarantees: tokens are delivered in order; we send a final completion event with metadata (model, total_tokens, finish_reason). If stop sequence triggers early finish, finish_reason = "stop".

7) Embeddings & reranker
- Embeddings: we recommend 512-2048 dim depending on model; batch sizes of 64-512 are efficient for Dedicated pools. Use incremental upserts to your vector DB; include document metadata to improve reranking signals.
- Reranker pattern: retrieve top-K via semantic search, then run a lightweight reranker model (or scoring network) over candidate passages. We offer a rerank endpoint that takes pairs or lists and returns scores; it’s cheaper than a full generation re-rank.

Resources attached: redwood-sdk-integration-guide.pdf (contains sample SDK auth flows, tokenization utility, and a sample response_format schema for a support ticket JSON). Marcus attached an example CSV mapping for your ingestion.

If this looks good I’ll flag a tech call slot next Wed/Thu. Also happy to produce a short security note for procurement.

— Neha

Neha — this is excellent, thanks. A couple quick clarifications so our security and infra teams can sign off: 

- For streaming: we prefer the direct-stream option if you support short-lived tokens with a 5-10 minute TTL. That fits best with our browser session model.
- For JSON strict mode: what happens to cost if the model needs multiple retries to produce valid JSON? We need an estimate for budgeting.

If you can add a short blurb in the security note about retry budgets + cost implications, and confirm token TTL options, we can move to procurement.

Samir
From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir@acme.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-06-22T09:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Acme integration — post-call recap + open questions

Samir / team — quick answers and attachments:  

- Direct-stream TTLs: we support configurable short-lived tokens down to 5 minutes; default templates show 1 minute for in-browser widgets and 10 minutes for server-to-server.
- JSON strict retry cost: retries are billed as separate generation calls. In strict mode we will do up to N retries (configurable; default 3) using progressively tighter prompts. Typical success rate for structured schemas is >90% within 2 tries, but we recommend a retry budget in procurement modeling (e.g., 1.25x expected generation cost for conservative planning).

Attaching: redwood-sdk-integration-guide.pdf and acme-mapping.csv (sample field mapping). I’ll also upload a 1-page security blurb to the Drive link Marissa included.

Next step: Marissa — can you propose two slots for next week for a 45-min technical deep dive?

— Marcus
